title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E443 studies the transverse vibrations of an elastic lamina (Euler–Bernoulli beam). The amplitude function on each segment is y = A cos(θx/b) + B sin(θx/b) + C e^{θx/b} + D e^{−θx/b}. On this page and the surrounding ones Euler treats a free–free lamina AB of length a, held at an interior point C by a pin (stylus). The pin divides the lamina into segments of lengths α and β. Each segment has its own coefficients (A,B,C,D) and (A',B',C',D'), with x and x' measured from the free ends A and B. The dimensionless lengths are ζ = θα/b and ζ' = θβ/b.

The eight conditions are:
- free ends (y'' = y''' = 0 at x = 0 and at x' = 0), four conditions;
- zero deflection at C on both sides, two conditions;
- continuity of slope at C (seventh equation);
- continuity of curvature at C (eighth equation, written as a sum because of the opposite orientation of x').

The free-end conditions give A = C + D and B = C − D. Then y(ζ) = 0 gives C/D = (−cos ζ + sin ζ − e^{−ζ})/(cos ζ + sin ζ + e^{ζ}). The analogous expression holds for C'/D'; this is the first display on the page.

Because general α:β makes the elimination hard, Euler specialises to the pin at the midpoint, β = α, so ζ = ζ' = θa/(2b). Then C/D = C'/D' = V, which gives A = D(1+V), B = D(V−1), and the same with primes.

Substituting into the seventh and eighth equations makes them factor. The seventh becomes (D−D')·[(V+1)sin ζ − (V−1)cos ζ − Ve^{ζ} + e^{−ζ}] = 0. The eighth becomes (D+D')·[(V+1)cos ζ + (V−1)sin ζ − Ve^{ζ} − e^{−ζ}] = 0. So either D' = −D or D' = D, giving two families of modes. In modern terms this is decomposing modes into those symmetric and antisymmetric about the pin.

Case I (D' = −D): the bracket of the seventh equation must vanish, i.e. y'(ζ) = 0. Together with y(ζ) = 0, each half behaves as a clamped–free cantilever of length a/2. On the next page, substituting V gives 2 = −cos ζ (e^{ζ} + e^{−ζ}), i.e. 1 + cos ζ cosh ζ = 0. I verified this algebra: the left side reduces to 4 + 2cos ζ (e^{ζ} + e^{−ζ}) = 0.

Case II (D' = D): y''(ζ) = 0, so each half is a pinned–free beam. The next page gives e^{2ζ} = (cos ζ + sin ζ)/(cos ζ − sin ζ), which is equivalent to tan ζ = tanh ζ.

Euler then remarks that the modes coincide with those of his principal problem (the cantilever) and of his second problem, each with half the length. He adds that several pins would be handled the same way.
errors: No substantive errors. Both factorizations and both frequency equations (1 + cos ζ cosh ζ = 0 and tan ζ = tanh ζ) are correct for the midpoint-pinned free–free beam.

The sign convention for the slope matching dy/dx = dy'/dx' with x' measured from the opposite end is consistent only with the matching orientation of y'. Euler handles curvature with an explicit sign argument but takes the slope condition without comment. The result is nevertheless consistent: case I correctly yields y'(ζ) = 0 at the midpoint.
In the last display the printed 'V+1.sin.ζ' means (V+1) sin ζ (old vinculum-style notation).

ideas.what: Free–free beam with an intermediate pin support; eight matching conditions (deflection zero, slope and curvature continuous; shear jump gives the pin reaction, which Euler declines to compute)
ideas.modern_name: Multi-span / intermediate-support beam vibration via transfer/matching conditions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E443, 1773); later systematic treatment by Rayleigh and in 20th-century structural dynamics
ideas.where_published: E443 itself (Novi Commentarii 17); discussed in Truesdell's Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11/2)

ideas.what: Splitting the modes of a midpoint-pinned beam into symmetric and antisymmetric families via D' = ±D
ideas.usually_credited_to: Commonly attributed to Rayleigh-era acoustics; Euler uses it here

ideas.what: Frequency equations 1 + cos ζ cosh ζ = 0 (clamped–free) and tan ζ = tanh ζ (pinned–free) recovered as the two halves
ideas.modern_name: Cantilever and pinned-free beam characteristic equations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (and D. Bernoulli for the cantilever, 1735–1744)
ideas.where_published: E443 and Euler's earlier elastic-curve work (E65 additamentum); Truesdell's account

deep.surprise_reason: These are correct and elegant classical results: the symmetry split giving cantilever and pinned–free half-beams. They are already published in E443 and covered by Truesdell's history of elasticity, so nothing appears to be missing from the record.
transcription_corrections: Last equation: 'V+1.sin.ζ' should be read as (V+1)sin ζ.
ζ = ζ' = θα/b = θa/(2b): the transcription is correct (the image shows 'θ a / 2 b').
